headline: ChatGPT Can Now Read and Send Your Text Messages

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called OpenAI makes a computer program called ChatGPT that can talk with people and answer questions. Now, OpenAI has made a new tool that connects ChatGPT to Apple Messages, which is the texting app on iPhones. This means ChatGPT can look at your text messages. It can help sort them, find old messages, suggest what to reply, and even send texts for you. Some people think this sounds helpful, like having a helper for your phone. But other people are worried, because text messages can have very private information in them, like secrets or personal stories. OpenAI says the tool works right on your phone or computer, not on a faraway server, and that it does not save a big list of all your messages. Still, some details about how it keeps things safe are not fully clear yet. OpenAI also tells users to always check messages before ChatGPT sends them, so that ChatGPT does not send something wrong by mistake. This story matters because more and more, computer programs are being trusted with private parts of our lives, like our conversations with friends and family.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, just released a new feature called a 'plug-in' that connects ChatGPT directly to Apple Messages, the texting app used on iPhones. A plug-in is like an add-on tool that lets one app work together with another. With this new connection, ChatGPT can read your texts, organize them, search through old conversations, and even write and send messages pretending to be you. OpenAI says this could save people time, especially at work, since the tool also works with business versions of ChatGPT. In an ad for the feature, a person asks ChatGPT to suggest replies to messages they got the day before. However, this raises a big question: how safe is your private information if a computer program can read all your texts? OpenAI told reporters that the tool runs on the user's own device, not on OpenAI's computers, and that it does not build a giant saved list of every message. But experts say the details of what that really means are still unclear. OpenAI also warns users not to let ChatGPT send messages automatically without checking them first, because that removes your last chance to catch a mistake. This story is important because it shows how AI is becoming more involved in personal, everyday parts of people's lives, and why people should think carefully about privacy before turning on features like this.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: OpenAI has launched a new plug-in that links ChatGPT to Apple's Messages app, giving the AI chatbot access to a user's private text conversations. Once connected, ChatGPT can sort messages, search through message history, analyze conversations, delete texts, and even draft and send new messages on a person's behalf. The tool isn't just for personal use either — it also works with Codex, an AI coding tool, and ChatGPT Work, a business version of the chatbot, meaning companies could use it too. A promotional video shows the AI reading yesterday's messages and suggesting thoughtful replies to send back. While this could make texting faster and easier, it also brings up serious privacy concerns, since text messages often contain sensitive personal details about relationships, health, finances, or private plans. OpenAI responded to these concerns by telling the news outlet Bloomberg that the plug-in runs locally, meaning it processes information directly on the user's own device rather than sending it to OpenAI's servers, and that it does not create a searchable index, or organized list, of everything someone has ever texted. However, exactly what that promise covers is still unclear, and journalists have asked OpenAI for more details. OpenAI is also urging caution around the message-sending feature specifically. The company recommends that users avoid turning on 'persistent approval,' a setting that would let ChatGPT send texts automatically without asking permission each time. OpenAI warns that skipping this review step removes a person's last chance to catch an error before a message goes out looking like it came from them. This story matters because it reflects a bigger trend of AI tools being given more direct access and control over people's personal accounts and communications. As AI becomes more capable of acting on someone's behalf, questions about trust, oversight, and data privacy become more urgent, especially since mistakes made by an AI sending a message could affect real relationships and reputations.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: OpenAI has introduced a new plug-in that connects its ChatGPT chatbot directly to Apple's Messages app, allowing the AI to interact with users' private text message histories. Through this integration, ChatGPT can organize messages, search for specific information buried in old conversations, analyze conversation patterns, delete unwanted texts, and even compose and send new messages on a user's behalf. The feature extends beyond personal use, since it also functions with Codex, OpenAI's AI coding assistant, and ChatGPT Work, its enterprise product, suggesting the company sees professional applications as well as personal ones. A promotional advertisement demonstrates the tool suggesting follow-up replies to contacts based on the previous day's conversations, framing the plug-in as a convenient productivity booster. Despite these potential benefits, the announcement immediately raises questions about digital privacy, since text messages frequently contain sensitive personal, financial, or relational information that users may not want processed by outside software, even indirectly. In response to these concerns, OpenAI told Bloomberg that the plug-in operates locally, meaning the data processing happens on the user's own device rather than being uploaded to OpenAI's remote servers, and that the tool does not construct a comprehensive index, or searchable database, of a person's entire message history. However, the company has not clarified exactly what technical safeguards exist or how thoroughly message data is protected, leaving some uncertainty about the true scope of privacy protection being offered. This ambiguity is significant, because vague or incomplete explanations from tech companies about data handling have historically preceded privacy controversies once more details emerge. Separately, OpenAI has issued a specific warning about the message-sending capability, cautioning users against enabling 'persistent approval,' a setting that would let ChatGPT send texts automatically without requiring the user to review each one beforehand. The company explicitly states that doing so eliminates a person's final opportunity to catch errors or inappropriate content before a message is sent under their name. This story is a notable example of the broader shift toward AI systems being granted increasing autonomy over personal communication tools, a trend that carries real consequences: if an AI misinterprets context or tone, it could send a message that damages relationships, embarrasses the user, or misrepresents their intentions, all without the person's direct involvement in that moment.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: OpenAI has released a plug-in, a software add-on that connects one application's capabilities to another, that links ChatGPT with Apple's Messages platform, effectively granting the chatbot access to users' private text conversation histories. Once integrated, the tool allows ChatGPT to sort and analyze messages, search for specific content within extensive conversation archives, delete texts, and autonomously draft and dispatch new messages on the user's behalf. Notably, this functionality extends beyond individual consumer use, as it is also compatible with Codex, OpenAI's AI-powered coding assistant, and ChatGPT Work, the company's enterprise-oriented product line, signaling that OpenAI anticipates both personal and professional adoption. A promotional demonstration showcases the AI generating contextually appropriate follow-up replies based on prior-day conversations, positioning the plug-in as a productivity-enhancing convenience rather than a niche experimental feature. This development, however, immediately surfaces substantive privacy considerations, given that text messages often constitute one of the most intimate records of a person's life, potentially containing financial details, health information, relationship dynamics, and other sensitive disclosures never intended for algorithmic processing. Addressing these concerns, OpenAI informed Bloomberg that the plug-in operates locally, meaning computation occurs directly on the user's device rather than transmitting data to OpenAI's remote infrastructure, and further stated that the system does not generate a comprehensive index, an organized, searchable catalog, of a user's complete messaging history. Nevertheless, the company has not provided granular technical detail clarifying precisely what safeguards govern data retention, encryption, or potential exposure, leaving meaningful ambiguity around the actual scope of user protection. This lack of specificity is consequential, since technology companies have historically offered reassuring but vague privacy language prior to subsequent revelations about data practices that contradicted initial claims. Additionally, OpenAI has issued a pointed caution regarding the message-composition feature, explicitly discouraging users from enabling 'persistent approval,' a configuration that would authorize ChatGPT to transmit messages automatically without requiring per-message user review. The company acknowledges that activating this setting eliminates the user's final safeguard, the opportunity to intercept and correct an erroneous, inappropriate, or misrepresentative message before it is sent under their identity. This episode exemplifies a broader industry trajectory in which artificial intelligence systems are increasingly entrusted with semi-autonomous control over deeply personal digital infrastructure, a shift that raises enduring questions about accountability, consent, and the adequacy of current safeguards. Should an AI system misjudge tone, context, or intent, the resulting consequences, whether reputational, relational, or professional, would be borne directly by the human user, even though the erroneous action originated from an automated process operating with only partial human oversight.

questions: If ChatGPT could read and send your texts, what parts of your private life do you think you would want to keep it away from, and why?
How might it change friendships or family relationships if people started letting AI write their text replies for them instead of writing their own?
Do you think companies like OpenAI give enough clear information about how they protect people's private data, and what more should they explain before people trust these tools?
